en: The Sadhana of Śrī Vajravārāhī. Oṃ! Homage to the illustrious Vajrayoginī!
To the lotus-feet of the illustrious Vajra Goddess...

O Vikramasena, having bowed down to Him by whom the bonds of the fetters of conceptualization have been severed, I shall diligently explain His means of accomplishment according to the instruction. (1)
In a cremation ground, in a mountain cave, near a river or the ocean,
or in some other most delightful location.
One should meditate upon this yoga for the attainment of desired success:
having visualized the seed-syllable *vaṃ* in the center of a lotus within the heart,
possessing the luster of a bandhūka flower.
One should see, all around, a multitude of Sugatas and others situated in the vault of the sky, illuminated by their rays;
[they appear] through the various [emanations] produced from the rays of those seed-syllables.
Having honored those deities with flowers and other offerings,
and having performed the sevenfold worship taught by the Jina, one should cultivate the contemplation of the four divine abodes. (4)
In that regard, the sevenfold worship is as follows: confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit,
going for refuge to the Three Jewels, dedication of merit, and the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Taking recourse to the path and the offering of one's own person—
this is the sequential exposition of the confession of sins and so forth, exactly as it is.
In the presence of these [beings], I confess all the evil that has been committed by me;
and whatever merit has been acquired by my teachers and others—
I rejoice in all of that—
whatever has been done, whatever will be done, and whatever I myself am doing—
so that by this merit, all sentient beings may become Victors.
I go for refuge to the Three Jewels; may I become a King of Dharma for the benefit of the world.
I take recourse in the path of the Victors.
"O Lords, take my own body; I give it to you.

(7) Furthermore, the four Brahma-vihāras are characterized by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). And these, in their proper sequence, are as follows:
just as people's conduct toward their own children [is directed].

Let them cultivate here that friendliness which, permeated with affection and characterized by constant conduct, would be the same toward the sons of others as it is toward their own, and which destroys hatred. (8)
Thus, he desires to uplift all the multitudes of beings from suffering and from that which serves as the cause of suffering.
One should cultivate that compassion toward all beings which serves as the antidote to a mind of malice;
for it is impossible to rescue infinite sentient beings [without it].
Thus, observing that even a worm became a Buddha through [the practice] skilled in destroying despondency, he generated vigor and cultivated sympathetic joy. (10)
That mind which has grown into the notions "this is mine" and "I am this" is indeed delusion;
it is the destroyer of that [delusion] because of the state of non-possession.
Reflect upon this equanimity:
because it is dependently arisen, one should see that which is false— both external and internal— as being like the moon reflected in water.
By reciting the mantra beginning with *svabhāvaśuddha*,
the practitioner of mantra should effect the meditative resolve upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In this regard, these are the two mantras:
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
Oṃ, I am of the essence of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Then, having visualized there a double-vajra (viśvavajra) born from the syllable *hūṃ*, with its mass of rays flashing forth in all directions,
one should [visualize] the earth and then the cage by means of that very [vajra].
One should visualize a canopy and a lattice of arrows;
having established the four mantras of Sumbha and others in the directions starting from the east and proceeding to the north, etc.
One should indeed place outside the four [goddesses] named after the walls, who originate from the network of rays of that [deity];
furthermore, the eight goddesses beginning with Kākāsyakā.
One should visualize [the goddesses] arising from the *sumbha* and other mantras,
having cast down the Māras into the wells of the eight *hūṃ*s, performing their beating and piercing. (15)
In that regard, these are the mantras: Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavān vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Here,
there are eight goddesses, namely: Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, Sūkarāsyā, Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathanī.
The instruction for this is as follows:
having placed the *coṭikā* with the thumb and forefinger of the left hand, [one recites] the mantras beginning with "Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha huṃ huṃ phaṭ."

While reciting [the mantra], one should sequentially arrange the vajra-fences— black, green, red, and yellow in color, with great flaming bodies pervading the netherworld and the entire universe— in a counter-clockwise direction starting from the east and the other cardinal points,
outside the cage.
The four goddesses beginning with Kakasī are produced from these four mantras;

at the very moment of their production, one should visualize the four goddesses beginning with Yamadāḍhī, who arise from the rays of light at the corners of the two mantras in the southward-turning clockwise direction starting from the southeast (Agni).
These eight [goddesses] have two arms and one face.
In this context, those below the navel are shaped like spikes;
they hold a vajra-hammer in their right hands and a kila in the form of themselves in their left hands.

Having gone forth by means of the yoga of radiation, one should summon the entire host of obstacles situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions; having caused them to enter the eight pits produced from the syllable *hūṃ* located near the ramparts and possessing the same color as one’s own mantra,
one should visualize that after the host of obstacles has been pinned and pounded— preceded by the recitation of the pinning and pounding mantras— they dissolve into the ramparts.
In this regard, the mantra for the ritual of staking is as follows: Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ | Oṃ kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ | Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands!
"Kīlaya the body, speech, and mind-vajras of all obstacles, hūṃ phaṭ! Thus is the mantra for striking. As for the mantra of the hammer: "Oṃ vajramudgara, strike the vajrakīla, hūṃ phaṭ!
Within that [vajra] lattice reside the charnel grounds...
One should visualize the Dharmodaya, situated in the center, with a form broad at the top, triangular, as white as the autumn moon, and containing a red lotus in its interior. (16)
Situated in the center of that lotus, between the sun and the moon, is the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, shining with a mass of radiating rays and possessing the luster of clear coral.
One should visualize [it] more clearly so that it becomes vivid:
having emerged from the web of rays produced from the seed-syllable,
one should cause the multitudes of beings to partake in the awakening of the Victors.
One should indeed thoroughly cultivate the [deities] beginning with the Buddha within that very seed-syllable placed inside. (18) (p.
Born from the seed-syllables of the Moon and Sun, she has three eyes,
the color of saffron, two arms, and one face;
she stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon the head and the tips of the breasts [of her victim].
[She stands] upon the two [gods] Bhairava and Kālarātri,
who lie supine; she drinks the stream of blood falling from a lotus-vessel held in her upraised left hand.
With her left hand, which holds a vajra and makes the earth-touching gesture, she threatens hosts of wicked beings; her left shoulder is beautifully adorned with a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Wearing a garland of fresh human heads hanging down with blood dripping from them,
naked, her feet adorned with tinkling anklets,
and bearing a face formidable with fangs; (21)
Her head was struck by a vajra preceded by a universal roar, causing her hair-knot to fall loose;
she shone amidst a garland of vajras.
She has five skulls situated upon the surface of her forehead; (22) (p.
238) her neck is beautiful with a wheel and swinging earrings.
With shimmering girdles of gold,
her head, ears, neck, both wrists, and the region of her hips were all brilliantly adorned with ornaments. (23)
She who shrouds the three worlds with her shimmering rays, whose body is pervaded by fresh youth,
and who is entirely filled with the essence of the form of great bliss.
One should assume the form of Vārāhikā as one's own body.
(24) Then, here, [one should place the mantras] at the navel, the heart, the mouth, the head, the crest-lock, and on all other limbs.
Having fashioned the armor with these six mantras, one should perform the entry into gnosis at the proper time. (25) These are the six mantras: Oṃ Vaṃ.
HĀṂ YOṂ,
HRĪṂ MOṂ, HREṂ HRĪṂ.
Huṃ huṃ, phaṭ phaṭ. These are the embodiments of Vajravārāhī, Yāminī, Mohinī, Sañcālinī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā.

Having worshipped with abundant flowers and other offerings produced by the rays of light from the syllable *vaṃ* situated in the wheel at the heart— [the deities] being red, blue, white, green, smoke-colored, and grey—
One should cause her, who abides in the sky, to enter into the pledge [of the consort], just as clarified butter enters clarified butter or water enters water. (26) (p.

Regarding the entry of the gnosis-being (jñānasattva), one should understand the four mantras— *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*— which perform the functions of summoning, entering, binding, and pleasing.
Having correctly beheld those Tathāgatas situated in the sky who bestow empowerment through these mantras, [one should proceed].
Behold Vairocana, born from the drops of water from the remaining consecration, seated upon the head.
(27) In this regard, the mantra for the consecration is as follows:
"Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth, so shall I bathe you with pure, divine water. (27i) "Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ."
In this regard, the instruction is as follows:
by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in the heart,

[the offerings are presented] by the eight Yoginīs who recite the sequence beginning with "Just as water [quenches] thirst" and ending with "by the water," while holding skull-cups in their left hands slightly tilted, filled with the five nectars.
Having visualized oneself as consisting of great bliss, being consecrated by streams of the nectar of one’s own primordial wisdom,
and having seen Vairocana arisen from the remaining water upon one’s head,
one should recite the mantra beginning with *oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka*.
Having seen the goddesses stationed in the sky honoring her and praising that Vārāhikā, [he...]
One should indeed taste the nectar accomplished through the sequence that is about to be described,
having reached every direction by means of emanation. (28)
Having performed all the activities for the benefit of the world, one should visualize one's own form entering the seed-syllable; thus one should act again and again until weariness occurs. (29)
Then, in order to bring his own mind to stability,
he should behold an extremely subtle, shimmering line of rays situated within the lunar and solar orbs at the navel.
That which is raised up by the extremely subtle resonance—
here, the yoga of non-apprehension is to be cultivated, having attained the path through the sequence of instruction.
For the sake of attaining luminosity, which serves as the cause for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings. (31) (p.
Having become weary of the practice of meditative elimination,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the supreme mantra according to the ritual procedure;
it is said to be comparable to a wish-fulfilling tree.
Having mastered that ten-syllable mantra by oneself through the power of the Victors,
one may then dwell as one pleases, free from weariness,
while maintaining the divine pride (*ahaṃkāra*) of one's own deity.
In this way, through constant application to recitation and meditation,
the yogin attains accomplishment within six months; however,
this applies to one who is unable to cultivate [the practice] without interruption.
He too would attain perfection if he were to practice momentary meditation at the proper times known as dawn, midday, and the evening twilight. (34)
In this regard, this is the ten-syllable heart mantra:
Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā.
The procedure for its recitation is as follows:
When weariness arises during meditation, one should quickly resolve upon the deity; then,
having visualized either a red syllable *vaṃ* or a *nāda* within the moon at her navel,
while reciting the mantra, [one should proceed].

Therefore, having emanated the assembly of goddesses from that *nāda* by means of the outgoing breath and having accomplished the welfare of the world, the mantra-practitioner, while reciting the mantra once again, should cause them to enter back into that very seed-syllable or *nāda* by means of the incoming breath— according to the principle of drawing in a thread together with a rosary.
He should do this repeatedly until fatigue occurs.
Of the circles of wind, fire, water, and earth, which have been meditated upon within that cage;
Alternatively, one may likewise visualize the Goddess situated upon the Mount Meru produced from her own seed-syllable.
This is the first stage of meditative cultivation. I.1.
One should visualize the four goddesses, Dākinī and the others, situated in the midst of the four skull-cups;
furthermore, one should visualize the eight goddesses with crow faces as being in addition [to them]. (36)
Or, the wise one should perform the visualization of Pracaṇḍā and the others seated upon the three wheels to a greater extent; thus, it becomes the Full Maṇḍala.
[One should visualize] Vajravārāhī residing in the wheel of great bliss.
Desiring to meditate upon her as accompanied by [the goddesses] Mā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī, who are situated in the eastern, northern, western, and southern directions,
he says:
"...the four goddesses situated in the midst of the four skull-cups.
Thus it has been said:

Likewise, one should place Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī in the positions of the directions of the lotus; they are the bestowers of all accomplishments. They are black, dark green, red, and fair-complexioned respectively, each having one face and four arms.
In their left hands they hold a skull-topped staff and a skull-cup; in their right hands, a hand-drum and a flaying knife.
They have three eyes, their hair is disheveled, and they stand in the *ālīḍha* posture.
Their faces are terrifying with bared fangs, and they are adorned with the five mudrās. (39–40)
"In the intermediate directions are four skull-cups [containing] the thought of awakening.
Thus, the group of four beginning with Ḍākinī should be understood as being sealed by Ratnasaṃbhava.
Therein, the heart mantra of the Bhagavatī is stated.
The subsidiary heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya*) is as follows: *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The eight-syllable mantra, however, is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī! Vaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the Noble Parājitā, Mother of the Three Worlds, Sovereign of Great Knowledge! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the one who brings fear to all beings, the Great Vajra! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the one seated on the vajra, the unconquered, the unconquerable, the subduer, the one who whirls the eyes! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the witherer, the wrathful, the furious, the terrifying! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to her who terrifies, who slays, who thoroughly pierces, who conquers—huṃ huṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to her who is victorious, who is more than victorious, who stupefies, who deludes—huṃ huṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to Vajravārāhī, the great yoginī, the mistress of desire, the sky-goer—huṃ huṃ phaṭ!
The mantras of the ḍākinīs and others are as follows:
Oṃ ḍākinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ lāme hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ khaṇḍarohe huṃ huṃ phaṭ | Oṃ rūpiṇīye huṃ huṃ phaṭ | Thus ends the second stage of meditation. 2.

(p. 252) Now, he speaks to one who wishes to meditate upon [the goddess] together with those situated at the eastern, northern, western, and southern gates of the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*)— namely, Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Sūkarāsyā— and with those situated in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners— namely, Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathanī:
"Or one should visualize the eight goddesses beginning with Kākāsyā as being predominant";
the four beginning with Kākāsyā have faces corresponding to their own names.
Yamadāḍhī and the others, however, have human faces and are of two colors.
These eight are sealed by Amoghasiddhi and are identical to Ḍākinī and the rest; their supreme distinction is their having a corpse as a seat. Thus it is said:
Just as it is for the host of *ḍākinīs*, so it is for those such as Kākāsyā, distinguished by their differences;
likewise are the goddesses situated in the intermediate directions,
for they possess two beautiful forms.
Seated upon corpses, most terrible, yet intent on accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
(41) Thus.
The mantras for these are as follows:
Oṃ kākāsye huṃ huṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ulūkāsye huṃ huṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ śvānāsye huṃ huṃ phaṭ | Oṃ sūkarāsye huṃ huṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamadāḍhīye huṃ huṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ yamadūtīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamadaṃṣṭriṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamamathanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Thus ends the third stage of meditative cultivation (bhāvanākrama). Now, he speaks— beginning with the words "Or else"— to one who wishes to cultivate the entire circle of goddesses (devīcakra) in its completeness.
By the term "three wheels" (*cakratraya*), the mind wheel (*cittacakra*), the speech wheel (*vākcakra*), and the body wheel (*kāyacakram*) are expressed. Therein,
in the sky in the eight directions of Mount Meru, is the mind wheel, which has eight spokes and is blue in color.
It is surrounded by a garland of blue vajras;
on its eastern, northern, western, and southern spokes—
in the places known as Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna, and Arbuda— respectively:

Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, and Mahānāsā are to be meditated upon in the spokes of the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, [corresponding to] the sites known as Godāvarī, Rāmeśvara, Devīkoṭa, and Mālava; [and] Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā [are to be meditated upon in the remaining spokes].
Thus is the wheel of mind (*cittacakra*).
This is the compendium of the *khecarīs*.
There, upon the circle of the earth, in the eight directions from Meru, is the red eight-spoked wheel of speech (*vākcakra*).
It is surrounded by a row of red lotuses.
On its eastern, northern, western, and southern spokes— in the regions known as Kāmarūpa, Oḍra, Triśakuni, and Kośala—
the goddesses Airāvatī, Mahābhairavā, Vāyuvegā, and Surābhakṣī are to be visualized.
In the spokes of the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast— known as Kaliṅga, Laṃpāka, Kāñcī, and Himālaya— reside Śyāmādevī, Subhadrā, Hayakarṇā, and Khagānanā.
This is the Wheel of Speech (vākcakra),
which is a compendium of the Earth-dwelling goddesses (bhūcarīs).
258) Then, upon the surface of the earth encircled by the ocean, there is the white body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) with eight spokes, surrounded by a series of white wheels.

On its eastern, northern, western, and southern spokes—located in the regions known as Pretapurī, Gṛhadevatā, Saurāṣṭra, and Suvarṇadvīpa—the goddesses Cakravegā, Khaṇḍarohā, Śauṇḍinī, and Cakravarmiṇī are to be meditated upon.
In the spokes of the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast—known as Nagara, Sindhu, Maru, and Kulata—reside Suvīrā, Mahābalā, Cakravartinī, and Mahāvīryā.
This concludes the body wheel (*kāyacakra*);
it is a compendium of those who dwell in the subterranean realm (*pātāla*).
There, the goddesses situated on the wheels of mind, speech, and body are, in order, black, red, and white, and are sealed by Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Vairocana.

All these goddesses, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, have one face and four arms; they hold a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup in their left hands and a curved knife and a ḍamaru drum in their right hands. They are three-eyed, with disheveled hair, naked, adorned with the five mudrās, wearing a garland of human heads hanging from their necks, and standing in the ālīḍha posture.

Then, at the level of the netherworld (pātāla), in the midst of the circles of fire and wind, one should visualize Kākāsyā and the others in the eight cremation grounds located in the eight directions of Mount Meru.
On the foreheads of all of them, including Vajravārāhī and the rest, there is a garland of vajras.
Now,
for the sake of attaining the identity with the deity and for the attainment of omniscience,
the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) should likewise be applied through union with the deity.
Furthermore, these factors are thirty-seven.

Among them, as antidotes to the four perversions—namely, purity, pleasure, permanence, and self—there are the four foundations of mindfulness (*anusmṛtyupasthāna*). They are as follows: the foundation of mindfulness of the body is Ḍākinī;
Lāmā is the application of mindfulness to feeling;
Khaṇḍarohā is the application of mindfulness to phenomena; Rūpiṇī is the application of mindfulness to the mind.
Memory is cognition that apprehends what has already been grasped; it is recollection,
and its "establishment" is that which brings it forth.

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), derived from the root with the meaning of the causative (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) due to the frequent usage [of the term]. Furthermore, because it brings to mind what was previously experienced,
it serves as the antidote to the forgetting of one's own virtues.
The body is the aggregate of the elements and the sense faculties;
sensation is the experience of pleasure and so forth;
and reality is the limit of existence.
The mind is mere appearance;
the recollection of these as being like an illusion is that which establishes it.
The foundations of mindfulness, beginning with the body;
the four bases of psychic power.
Therein, Chanda-ṛddhipāda is Pracaṇḍā, Vīrya-ṛddhipāda is Caṇḍākṣī,
and Mīmāṃsā-ṛddhipāda is Prabhāvatī.
"The basis of psychic power is the great nose"—thus [it is said].
*Chanda* is the longing for hearing and so forth regarding the sphere of the True Dharma.
*Ṛddhi* is success; it is the concentration of the mind.

Its "feet" (pāda) are its limbs; thus, it is a *vigraha-samāsa* (analytic compound) meaning "this is both desire (*chanda*) and a basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). The same should be understood for the basis of psychic power consisting of energy (*vīrya*), and so forth.
By the rule "ṛtyaka," there is no *guṇa* substitution due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
Vigor (*vīrya*) is the mental enthusiasm for wholesome action; investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) is thorough examination.
The mind is knowledge.
That in the presence of which knowledge exercises its power is a faculty (*indriya*), such as the eye and so forth.
By analogy with these, faith and the other [faculties] are also called faculties.
That is fivefold, namely: the faculty of faith is Vīramatī,
and the faculty of vigor is Kharvarī.
The faculty of mindfulness is Laṅkeśvarī, the faculty of concentration is Drumacchāyā, and the faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī.
In that regard, vigor has been explained,
and mindfulness has also been explained.
Faith (*śraddhā*), however, is the clarity of mind regarding mundane and supramundane right view and the enjoyment of the fruits of karma.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the intellect that discerns what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.

The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) is that which brings forth and presents those phenomena (*dharma*) based upon the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetting of the object presented by energy.
The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) is that which brings face-to-face those phenomena based upon the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is that which penetrates those phenomena which have been made one-pointed by the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
These very faculties, when they reach excellence through degrees of intensity and so forth, are called powers (*bala*).
For example, the power of faith (*śraddhābala*) is Mahābhairavā.
The power of vigor is Vāyuvegā;
the power of mindfulness is Surābhakṣī;
the power of concentration is Śyāmādevī.
And Subhadrā is the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*).
The factors of perfect enlightenment (*sambodhyaṅga*) are the causes of right awakening;
furthermore, they are seven.
Namely: Hayakarṇā is the factor of enlightenment of concentration; Khagānanā is the factor of enlightenment of vigor;
Cakravegā is the factor of enlightenment of joy.

The limb of awakening of pliancy is Khaṇḍarohā; the limb of awakening of discrimination of phenomena is Śauṇḍinī; the limb of awakening of mindfulness is Cakravarmiṇī; and the limb of awakening of equanimity is Suvīrā.
Samādhi is one-pointedness of mind;
it is a compound formed by analyzing [the term] as "that which is both samādhi and a factor of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*).
In this same way, it should be understood regarding the factors of enlightenment (*saṃbodhyaṅga*) and so forth:
vigor is the absence of opportunity for laziness;
joy is the one-pointedness of the mind upon phenomena (*dharma*).

Pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) is the state of body, speech, and mind being intent upon wholesome action due to the eradication of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of "self" and "mine" and so forth. The discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is the ascertainment of all phenomena by way of their selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetfulness of the vow for perfect awakening for the sake of all sentient beings, as well as [the teachings on] hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is a state of mental indifference.

Because it serves as the antidote to the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the eight factors beginning with right view are "noble" (*ārya*); that which possesses these is the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*).
The path (*mārga*) is that which is sought and pursued for the sake of cultivating the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Its limbs are as follows: right view is its great strength, and right intention is its sovereign wheel-turner (*cakravartinī*).
Right speech is Mahāvīryā,
right action is Kākāsyā,
and right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā.
Right effort is Śvānāsyā,
right mindfulness is Sūkarāsyā,
and right concentration is the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī.
In that regard, supreme reverence for the word of the Buddha is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Not abandoning an undertaking once it has been begun is right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
Speech that does not deceive regarding the welfare of sentient beings is right speech (*samyagvāk*).

Right action (*samyak-karmānta*) is activity that does not transgress the ten wholesome paths of action. Right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) is maintaining one's life with wealth acquired through righteous means.
Right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) is the activity of body, speech, and mind for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others.
The recollection of the Buddha’s word is right mindfulness;
the focal point on the form of Śrī Vajravārāhī is right concentration.
They are called the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) because by means of them, passion and the other afflictions are correctly abandoned; there are four of them, namely:
the production of wholesome states (*dharma*) that have not yet arisen, which is *yamadaṇḍī*;
and the protection of wholesome states that have already arisen, which is *yamadūtī*.
The abandonment of unwholesome states that have already arisen is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and the non-arising of unwholesome states not yet arisen is Yamamathanī.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme maṇḍala of the body.

Through the sequential yoga of the *pīṭhas* and so forth, by means of the purification of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), [the following sequence is established]: *pu*, *jā*, *o*, *a*, *go*, *rā*, *de*, *mā*, *kā*, *o*, *tri*, *ko*, *ka*, *la*, *kā*, *hi*, *pre*, *gṛ*, *sau*, *su*, *na*, *si*, *ma*, *ku*. Such is the tradition (*āgama*).
The meaning here is as follows: the initial syllables of Pullīramalaya and so forth—beginning with *puṃ* and others—are pronounced together with their nasalization (*anusvāra*).

One should immediately understand that the wheels (*cakras*) at the front are voids (*śūnya*) transformed from the initial syllables such as *puṃ*, and that the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) and other locations, such as Pullīramalaya, correspond to the head and other parts of the body.
The channels situated within those [parts], beginning with the head, are to be meditated upon as being established through the transformation into deities such as Pracaṇḍā and the others.
One should contemplate Caṇḍā, preceded by Pra, situated on the head at Pullīramalaya;
one should meditate upon Caṇḍākṣī at the crest-lock in Jālandhara;
and one should visualize Prabhāvatī at Oḍḍiyāna from the right ear. (43)
One should visualize Arbudi on the back of the head as Mahānāsā;
thus is the seat Pramuditā-bhūmi.
One should contemplate Godāvarī on the left ear and Vīramatī [on the right].
Behold Kharvarī stationed at Rāmeśvara and between the eyebrows;
behold this Laṅkeśvarī at the corners of the eyes of the goddesses.
On both shoulders is declared that which is known as the Mālava country. (45)
There, one should indeed meditate upon the Goddess whose name is Drumacchāyā.
(46) Thus [ends] the secondary seat (upapīṭha), the Vimalā stage.

One should meditate on this Airāvatī in the two armpits in Kāmarūpa; likewise, one should meditate on the goddess Mahābhairavikā in Oḍra and on both breasts. (47) Thus is the sacred field, the stage of Prabhākarī.
One should perceive Vāyuvegā, with flickering luster, at the navel;
likewise, one should perceive Surābhakṣī at the tip of the nose in Kośala.
Thus is the Upakṣetra, the Arciṣmatī Bhūmi.
One should visualize the goddess named Śyāmā in the face in Kaliṅga,
and likewise the goddess Subhadrā in the region of the throat in Lampāka. (49) Thus ends the section on the Chando-ha, the Abhimukhī stage.
One should visualize the goddess Hayakarṇā in the heart at Kāñcī,
and likewise this Khagānanā in the region of the Himālaya at the penis. (50) Thus, through these two secondary meters, the stage is Sudurjayā.
In the city of the pretas, one should remember Cakravegā of radiant luster at the linga;
she who is the deity of the house is Khaṇḍarohikā in the anus.
Thus concludes the meeting on the stage of Dūraṅgamā (Far-reaching).
In the city, she is the yoginī named Suvīrā among the finger-joints;
at her feet in Sindhu is that yoginī of great power. (52)
Thus, the cremation ground is the stage Sādhumatī.
One should meditate on the Yoginī Cakravartinī at the two big toes in Maru;
likewise, Mahāvīryā is considered to be at the two knees in Kulatā. (53)
Thus ends the *upaśmaśāna*, the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
Kākāsyā and the others are situated respectively in the mouth, the navel, the genitals, and the anus;
likewise, Yamadāḍhī and the others are in the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft, the ears, the eyes, and the nose. (55)
The four goddesses, beginning with Ḍākinī, abide taking recourse in the heart;
thus, one should always contemplate this supreme body-maṇḍala in its entirety. (56)
Just as in the external world they provide nourishment through water at places such as *pīṭhas* along a river, so too within the body do the flowing rivers nourish the nails and other parts.
Externally, the *vajrapīṭha* is the site of great awakening,
and the river is the *Nirañjanā*.
Within the body, however, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is considered to be the adamantine seat (*vajrapīṭha*), the central channel (*avadhūtī*), and the stainless (*nirañjana*).
Now, the mantras of the deities are stated.
Among them, the heart, near-heart, and eight-line mantras of Vajravārāhī have been taught.

Her root mantra is stated as follows: Oṃ namo bhagavati vajravārāhi vaṃ— O unconquered one, mother of the three worlds, sovereign of great knowledge, bringer of fear to all beings, great thunderbolt, wielder of the vajra-thunderbolt, unconquered and invincible, subduer, whirler of eyes, witherer, wrathful one, furious one, terrifying one, crusher, excellent divider, conqueror, victorious, most victorious, paralyzer, and immobilizer!
Mohani, Vajravārāhī, Mahāyoginī, Kāmeśvarī, Khage—
O lofty one! Strike, strike the life-breaths!

Kiṅi kiṅi! Khiṅkhiṇi khiṅkhiṇi! Shake, shake, O you who hold a vajra in your hand! Dry up, dry up, O you who bear the vajra-khaṭvāṅga and skull-bowl! O devourer of great flesh and meat! O you clothed in human entrails! Be present, O Sumbha and Nisumbha!

Destroy, destroy my evil and that of all sentient beings and all animals! O you who cut off the great flesh, O wrathful form, O terrible fang-bearer, O Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), O foremost queen of the deity Śrī Heruka, you with a thousand necks, a thousand arms, and a hundred thousand faces, blazing with splendor, O flame-mouthed one, tawny-eyed one, diamond-bodied one, seated on a diamond throne, *mili mili*, *timili timili*, *he he he he*, *huṃ huṃ*, *kha kha*, *dhu dhu*, *ru ru*!

Dhuru dhuru muru muru! O non-dual Great Yoginī, perfected through recitation! Oṃ dhraṃ! He he ha ha! O Fierce One! Hasa hasa hā hā ho ho hūṃ hūṃ! O Destroyer of the Three Worlds! O You who are surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of Tathāgatas! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! O You in the form of a lion! Khaḥ! O You in the form of an elephant! Āḥ! O You whose belly is the three worlds! O You whose girdle is the great ocean!

Grasa grasa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! O you who are non-dual with the Hero, hūṃ hūṃ hā hā! O you who delude the great beast! You are Mahāyogeśvarī, the Ḍākinī who is worshipped by all the worlds, who produces immediate conviction, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! O terrifier of spirits!
*Mahāvīre paramasiddhayogeśvari phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Thus the mantras of the Ḍākinīs and so forth have been stated,
as well as those of the eight [faced goddesses] beginning with Kākāsyā.
The mantras for Pracaṇḍā and the others follow the sequence of the *kuliśapada* (vajra-step), as follows:
Oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kuru kuru...
Caṇḍākṣīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ bandha bandha prabhāvatīye.
Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, terrify, terrify, O Great Destroyer, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, agitate!
Oṃ hreṃ hreṃ, to Kharvarī, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hraḥ hraḥ oṃ pheṃ pheṃ, to Drumacchāyā, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ phaṭ phaṭ, to Airāvatī, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ daha daha, to Mahābhairavī, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ paca paca, to Vāyuvegā, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ bhakṣa bhakṣa, O you who hang from a garland of blood and entrails, O drinker of wine, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa, seize the serpent or snake dwelling in the seven nether worlds; threaten, threaten, O Śyāmādevī, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ ākarṣa ākarṣa, draw [them] forth, O Subhadrā, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hayakarṇe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ jloṃ jloṃ khagānane huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kṣyāṃ kṣyāṃ cakravege huṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ khaṇḍarohe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hiṃ hiṃ śauṇḍinīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ huṃ hūṃ cakravarmiṇīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ kili kili suvīre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ sili sili mahābale huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ cili (p. 284)
*Ci-li cakravartinī-ye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ dhili dhili mahāvīrye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |* In these mantras of Pracaṇḍā and the others, the first *hūṃ* syllable is short.
The second [syllable] is long;
this should be understood from the oral instruction of the guru. However, according to the view of Bhavyācārya and others, it is: "Oṃ pracaṇḍe huṃ huṃ phaṭ."

"Oṃ Caṇḍākṣi huṃ huṃ phaṭ," and so forth—these will be stated to be their mantras; for indeed, the meaning of this scripture was demonstrated by them as follows: "The utterance of one's own name, joined with the syllables *huṃ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*, [constitutes the mantra]."
The mantra for these yoginīs consists of their own names;
the supreme oṃkāra should be placed at the beginning, and the syllables huṃ huṃ phaṭ should be placed at the end.
This has been shown by the passage beginning with "one's own name" (*svanāma*).
Thus ends the fourth stage of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*).
All the ritual procedures for worship and so forth, whatever they may be, that are proclaimed in the scriptures (*āgama*), [are to be understood in this way].
Those [rites] preceded by the offering of bali should be performed by those desiring success.
Since it is held that the bali should be offered by one joined with the yoga of the deity, this bali is therefore taught to follow after that yoga. (57–58)
In that regard, the tasting of the nectar of power (*balimṛtāsvādana*) is described as follows:
the wind mandala, born from the black syllable *yaṃ*, has the appearance of a bow.
Above that, in the center, is a red circle of fire born from the syllable RAṂ.
Situated above that is a white skull-cup born from the syllable ĀḤ, serving as a hearth fashioned by three heads arising from the three stepped [pedestals]. (59–60)

One should contemplate the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth as being born from seed-syllables such as *oṃ*, presided over by them, and situated within a skull-cup (*karoṭa*) in their respective forms, beginning with blood.
(61) Regarding "and so forth": *oṃ āṃ jrīṃ khaṃ hūṃ lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ* are the seed-syllables of the five Tathāgatas and the four goddesses.
Seeing that which was born from the seed, melted there by the heat of the wind-blazing fire,
possessing a luster resembling the color of a pomegranate flower, (62) (p.

Then, one should visualize that within the white khaṭvāṅga produced from the syllable *hūṃ*, which faces downward and consists of nectar, there is a white, cool liquid resulting from the dissolution [of the syllable]. Above that,
[one should see] the emergence from the transformation of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*).

From this mantra—*oṃ āḥ hūṃ*—which stands sequentially one above the other, the wheel of deities emanates; having performed the benefit of sentient beings, they dissolve and enter into the three syllables, and those three syllables likewise enter into the nectar. (64–65)
One should visualize that nectar as a liquid, presided over by the three syllables.
When that has been accomplished, one should offer the bali-oblation according to this rite:

having brought the circle of deities with the flame-gesture (*jvālāmudrā*), the *phetkāra*-sound, and the gesture of fearlessness, and having worshipped them preceded by the water-offering (*argha*) and other rites—
All phenomena are mutually interpenetrating; all phenomena are mutually infused. Preceded by the recitation of the mantra *hūṃ*, [one visualizes] two *hūṃ* syllables mounted upon the moon and sun.

Having transformed [the palms] into vajra-añjali and placed a vessel of nectar thereon, or having meditated upon it, one should recite this for the sake of attaining the desired siddhi: "The goddesses are the authority, the samaya is the authority, and their spoken words are the supreme authority.
By this truth, may these goddesses become the cause of my grace."
Thus, one should perceive the object of worship, the act of worship, and the worshipper as non-different. Then,

while rotating the vessel counter-clockwise through the cardinal directions starting from the east and clockwise through the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, one should offer that nectar while reciting the two mantras of the deities whose tongues are vajras born of the syllable *hūṃ*.
In this regard, the mantra is: Oṃ kara kara,
kuru kuru.
Bind, bind!
Terrify, terrify!
Agitate, agitate!
Hrauṃ hrauṃ, hraḥ hraḥ,
pheṃ pheṃ.
Phaṭ phaṭ! Burn, burn! Cook, cook!
Eat, eat! O you who hang from a garland of human flesh, blood, and entrails!
Seize, seize!
Threaten, threaten the serpent or snake that has gone to the seventh underworld; pull it out, pull it out!
Hrīṃ hrīṃ,
jloṃ jloṃ,
kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ.
hāṃ hāṃ,
hiṃ hiṃ,
kili kili.
sili sili, ḍhili ḍhili, dhili dhili,
HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ. This mantra should be recited once. Thereafter—
Oṃ vajrāralli hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ, vajraḍākinyas, you are the samaya, appear! Hoḥ! This is the mantra.

Having recited [the mantra] one, two, three, four, or five times, one should offer the nectar (*amṛta*). Then, having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and other rites, one should recite this verse for the sake of attaining one's desired goal: "O you whose attachment is equal to the cessation of existence, who have shattered the obstacles to one's resolve..."
Perceiving all existence as being like space in its true nature,
you whose ocean-like minds are swollen with the waters of profound compassion— O Goddesses, bestow upon me the utmost mercy! (69)
Thus it is said.

Then, while reciting the mantra two or three times as before, one should offer nectar to the guardians of the directions and other deities stationed in the eight cremation grounds, moving [the vessel] through the cardinal and intermediate directions.

In this regard, the mantra is as follows: Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali offering; protect the pledge (samaya); grant me all accomplishments (siddhi)! Eat, drink, and smell according to your own pleasure and desire; do not transgress! Be my helpers in every way for the increase of true happiness! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
*Svāhā*. Thus, the guardians of the directions (*dikpālāḥ*), being satisfied, should be visualized as bestowing accomplishment upon the practitioner.

Thereafter, having offered betel leaves and other items to them collectively, and having performed the *saṃcchomya* gesture with the *chomaka* hand, one should first recite while ringing the bell with the left hand for the purpose of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure.
This mantra:
Oṃ vajraheruka, protect the samaya; abide as Heruka!
Be firm for me;
be easy to satisfy for me; be easy to nourish for me.
Be devoted to me;
grant me all accomplishments;
and in all actions, make my mind auspicious, hūṃ!
Ha ha ha ha hoḥ! O Blessed One, Vajraheruka, do not abandon me! Become Heruka, the Great Samaya-being! Āḥ hūṃ phaṭ!

Thus it is said. Then, reciting "Oṃ, all phenomena are purified by yoga; I am purified by yoga," and having satisfied [the deities] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā, one should perform the gesture of embracing upon the withdrawal of that mudrā.
Then, preceded by snapping the ring finger and thumb, one should dismiss [the deities] while reciting the mantra "Oṃ mur," and cause that maṇḍala-circle to enter into oneself.
Now, the procedure for the external worship is described:
Having risen in the morning, the yogi, established in the yoga of his own deity, places his left hand on a clean spot and recites the four mantras beginning with "Oṃ sumbha ni-sumbha.

Then, using a pill made of the five nectars (*pañcamṛta*) and perfumes, or—if the five nectars and so forth are unavailable—mixed with any other substance or mixed with cow dung, he draws a circular mandala with a triangle in its center.

Having placed the syllable *vaṃ*, which has emerged from the heart, upon the red lotus-stalk situated in the center of that [maṇḍala], one should visualize the Blessed Lady—who is of the nature of primordial wisdom—invoked by the rays of light from that seed-syllable, made to enter the *vaṃ*, and transformed into the Blessed Lady.

Then, having worshipped her with flowers and other offerings issued from the seed-syllable in the heart, one should offer a flower with the left hand purified according to the ritual while reciting the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*; thereafter, [one should worship] with the heart-mantra, the upahr̥daya-mantra, and the eight lines.
And one should offer flowers. Thereafter,
having worshipped the guardians of the directions and others situated in the cremation ground with the three-syllable mantra, one should worship them by interlacing their names [with the mantra].
Then, one should offer flowers with their respective mantras, beginning with *oṃ ha*, as will be described, to the deities placed in the left hand at their respective locations.
Having first cast [the flowers] into the maṇḍala and formed a handful of flowers over one's head, one should cause the wheel of deities residing in the left hand to enter into oneself.
Then, one should perform praise with the eight-line heart-mantras and other hymns.

Having performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth, and having performed the meditations, recitations, and aspirations and so forth, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra in order to fill any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure.
Thereafter: *oṃ yogaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā yogaśuddho 'ham*.

Having thus gratified [the deity] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā preceded by the recitation of the mantra, and having performed the gesture of embracing upon the withdrawal of that mudrā, and having snapped the fingers while touching the ground, one should dismiss that deity with the mantra *oṃ mur* and cause her to enter into oneself. Then, one should erase the lines of the maṇḍala.
300) In this manner, by way of this direction, the sequence of worship for the deities in the second and subsequent stages of meditative cultivation should be inferred by oneself.
Now, the procedure for the hand-worship is described.

In the maṇḍala of the gaṇa and other such settings, the mantra-practitioner, joined with his chosen deity, [visualizes] upon the six— the nails of the left hand’s thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger, little finger, and [the back of] the hand— the forms of Vajrasattva, Vairocana, Amitābha, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi, respectively, in the colors white, white, red, black, yellow, and dark green. Oṃ ha, nama hi.
Svāhā huṃ, vauṣaṭ he,
huṃ huṃ ho, phaṭ haṃ.
Thus one should place the mantras.
Having visualized a red five-petalled lotus instantly formed within the palms of the hands, one should perceive the seed-syllable "Oṃ Vaṃ" in the form of Vajravārāhī in the center of the pericarp.

On the petals in the east, north, west, south, and the intermediate corners, in due order, are the forms of Yāminī, Mohinī, Saṃcālinī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā, colored blue, white, yellow, green, and smoky-grey respectively.
Haṃ yoṃ, hrīṃ moṃ, hreṃ hrīṃ.
One should visualize the seed-syllables "huṃ huṃ" and "phaṭ phaṭ.
One should see this reflection of the seed-syllables held in the hand as the three wheels (tricakra) shimmering upon the back of the hand below.

Then, having smeared all the seed-syllables held in one's hands with a liquid substance and having visualized the palm of the hand as being presided over by all the yoginīs, one should offer that liquid and other substances with the three-syllable mantra or the eight-line mantra.

Then, having performed the worship and recited the hundred-syllable mantra for the purpose of filling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure, [one should do so] for the sake of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vajrayoginī.

Having requested [permission] with the words, "The goddesses are the authority; the *samaya* is the authority," and so forth, one should place the substance held in that hand into another substance or vessel,
and then, with the substance held in the hand, grasped by the left ring finger—
Having uttered "HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ" over the heart, tongue, and head while anointing [them], one should resolve that the host of deities has entered into oneself;
this procedure, however, is to be understood as taught in the *Saṃcāra-tantra*.

Alternatively, having formed a triangular mandala on the ground by circling counter-clockwise with the ring finger of the left hand—which has been purified according to the previously mentioned procedure—using the *madanaphala* (jujube fruit) thus purified, one should visualize Vajravārāhī, produced from the seed-syllable emerging from the heart, adorned by the eight cremation grounds. Having offered to her the food and other items prepared in the form of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, using either the three-syllable mantra or the eight-word mantra, [one should offer] the substance contained within the lotus-vessel and so on.
Taking the nectar-like *madana* with the thumb and ring finger, one should satisfy the Blessed Lady with the three-syllable mantra, the heart-mantra, the near-heart-mantra, and the eight-line mantra.
One should satisfy the deities of the cremation ground with the three-syllable mantra.

Having thus performed the worship, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra to fill any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure. Then, having made the request as before for the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the deity, [one should reflect that] all phenomena are purified through yoga.

Reciting "I am purified by yoga," he should satisfy [the deity] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā; then, withdrawing the mudrā and preceded by the gesture of embracing (*liṅgana*), he should dismiss the deity into himself with three snaps of the fingers and the syllable "Oṃ mur.
Thereafter, taking the *madana* (wine) that has settled on the ground with the ring finger of the left hand, he should smear it upon his heart, tongue, and head while uttering "Hūṃ Āḥ Oṃ."
One should visualize even the circle of deities held in the hand as having entered into oneself.
In this manner, by way of this direction, one should worship the deities with their respective mantras during the second and subsequent stages of meditative cultivation.

Thereafter, one should perform the internal fire offering (*adhyātmahoma*) as follows: [one visualizes] a white tongue made from the transformation of a white *hūṃ* syllable; with the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) in the right hand, one offers the oblation into the Goddess who resides upon the pericarp of one’s own navel-lotus and is surrounded by garlands of flames.
Thereafter: *oṃ āḥ ucchiṣṭavajrādhitiṣṭhemaṃ baliṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
With this mantra, one should consecrate the offering of the remnants (ucchiṣṭabali) after going outside.
Now, the cremation ground previously mentioned is described:
In the northeastern direction, associated with Varuṇa,
lies the cremation ground of Yāmeśvarā;
there is also the one named Caṇḍogra and the Gahvara.
And [the cremation grounds] named Karaṅkaka and Subhīṣaṇa;
in these cremation grounds, there shall be trees in sequence: the śirīṣa, the bodhi, the kaṅkeli, and the cūta.
Indra, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Yama are to be known as the lords of the directions beginning with the East and the intermediate corners. (71) Śrī Vāsuki and the one named Takṣaka [are also there].
The nāgas Karkoṭa and Padma are here;
these clouds are Garjita-ghūrṇita and the terrible one called Āvartaka. (72)

Likewise, the second was named Lakṣmīvana; the third was Ghorāndhakāra, which truly lived up to its name; and the fourth was indeed called Ārava, preceded by the sound "ā-ra. (74)
The trees, in order, are the *trivaṭa*, the *karañja*, the beautiful creeper, the *parkaṭī*, and the *arjuna*;
[these are associated with] Īśāna, Vaiśvānara, and Jātudhāna.
Know the Prabhāñjanas to be the lords of the corners.
As for the Nāgas, they are Padma, distinguished by his greatness,
Hulur (repeated twice), Kulika, and Śaṅkha.
One [cloud] is solid, two are full of rain, and the fourth is fierce; these are the clouds.
Having performed this, my merit has been accumulated.
May they, by this merit as white as the rays of the autumn moon,
having destroyed all defects of conceptual construction, attain the state of the illustrious Vajradevī. (77)
The sādhana of Śrīvajravārāhī is completed.
This work is the composition of the venerable scholar and great preceptor, the illustrious Umāpatideva.
